group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 54-year-old man presented this morning to the peri-operative internal medicine service at the request of his urologic surgeon for evaluation prior to an elective laparoscopic left adrenalectomy scheduled in two weeks for a 3.2-cm hormonally inactive incidentaloma discovered on imaging of the abdomen performed to investigate vague flank discomfort; he reports no catecholamine-associated spells, cushingoid features, or electrolyte disturbances, and surgical planning anticipates a brief overnight stay if there are no complications. He arrived on foot from the parking lot, carrying his medical records without assistance, and states that during a typical workday as a postal carrier he walks several city blocks, climbs two flights of stairs to sort mail, and lifts parcels weighing up to 20 lb without dyspnea, palpitations, or chest pressure. His only cardiometabolic illness of significance is long-standing diabetes mellitus first diagnosed at age 14; he self-manages with a hybrid basal-bolus insulin strategy consisting of 28 units of insulin degludec subcutaneously each evening and correction doses of insulin aspart with meals guided by a continuous glucose sensor. Review of his downloads over the past month demonstrates fasting glucose values varying between 95 mg/dL and 160 mg/dL, with no nighttime hypoglycemia alarms. He denies any episodes of diabetic ketoacidosis since adolescence. Hypertension is present and treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily and chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, yielding home blood pressures in the 120s/70s. Hyperlipidemia is managed with rosuvastatin 40 mg nightly. There is background mild non-proliferative retinopathy followed by ophthalmology but no visual impairment, and he wears custom-molded insoles for sensory neuropathy manifested by diminished vibration sense in his toes. He categorically denies hospitalizations or emergency visits for fluid overload, has never been told he had a murmur or cardiomyopathy, and has not experienced orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, unexplained weight gain, or exercise intolerance. He similarly reports no prior episodes suggestive of myocardial ischemia such as exertional chest discomfort, jaw pain, or radiation to the arm, and he has never undergone coronary angiography, stress testing, or revascularization procedures. Respiratory history is notable only for well-controlled mild intermittent asthma requiring albuterol two or three times per month during pollen season; he has never smoked cigarettes or used vaping devices. There is no personal or family history of premature atherosclerotic events; his father died at 82 of colon cancer, and his mother is alive at 80 with osteoporosis. He consumes one or two light beers on weekends and does not use recreational drugs. Allergies are limited to seasonal grasses; he tolerates contrast media and latex. Systems review is otherwise unrevealing for syncope, transient neurologic symptoms, claudication, night sweats, fevers, bleeding diathesis, or easy bruising. After five minutes seated, vital signs are: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg in the right arm, pulse 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air; body mass index is 27 kg/m². He appears well hydrated and in no distress. Jugular venous contour is not elevated at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruits, and the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced. Heart sounds are crisp S1 and S2 with no S3, S4, murmurs, clicks, or rubs. Lungs are clear to auscultation throughout with good air movement. Abdomen is soft; a firm but non-tender left adrenal fullness is not palpable, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Extremities show no edema; peripheral pulses are 2+ and symmetric. A focused neurologic examination reveals intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups, normal light touch, diminished vibratory sense in the distal toes, and a steady tandem gait. Pre-operative laboratories drawn one hour before the encounter demonstrate hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, elevated from a baseline of 1.7 mg/dL six months ago but stable for several years and attributed to long-standing diabetic nephropathy with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 41 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting glucose in the same sample is 142 mg/dL; albumin-to-creatinine ratio from last month was 220 mg/g. Liver enzymes, bilirubin, and coagulation studies are within reference limits. A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram performed today shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, normal intervals, and no pathologic Q waves, ST-segment deviations, or T-wave inversions. A transthoracic echocardiogram obtained nine months earlier for baseline diabetic evaluation recorded left ventricular ejection fraction of 60 %, normal wall thickness, and no valvular pathology. Chest radiograph this morning demonstrates clear lung fields and normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Anesthesia examination notes Mallampati class II airway, full cervical extension, and an inter-incisor distance of 4.5 cm. He has been instructed to continue all usual antihypertensive and statin therapy up to the day of surgery, to reduce the evening basal insulin dose by 20 % the night before the procedure, omit rapid-acting insulin on the morning of surgery unless fasting glucose exceeds 200 mg/dL, and monitor point-of-care capillary glucose upon arrival to the pre-operative holding area. He verbalizes understanding of nil-per-os instructions after midnight, postoperative incentive spirometry, early ambulation, and the importance of glycemic control to wound healing.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) gives 1 point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular): the adrenal gland is retroperitoneal, and a transperitoneal approach is not specified. Without assuming that approach, score 0.
- Ischemic heart disease: no history of ischemia or revascularization and no pathologic Q waves = 0.
- Heart failure: no history or clinical findings of heart failure = 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA documented = 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: uses basal insulin degludec and mealtime insulin aspart = 1.
- Creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: admission value 1.9 mg/dL does not meet the threshold despite diabetic nephropathy = 0.
Total = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 1.
Final answer: 1
